entities.name: Methodist Episcopal Church
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Methodist Episcopal Church, founded in Baltimore in 1784 as the American Methodist organization organized by Francis Asbury and Thomas Coke after the American Revolution, was America's largest Protestant denomination from approximately 1820 to 1850 and the institutional force that evangelized the American frontier through the circuit rider system. The church's 1844 split over slavery — creating northern and southern Methodist bodies — was the largest Protestant schism in American history before the Civil War and anticipated the political division that would cause the war itself.

John Wesley sent Thomas Coke and Francis Asbury to organize American Methodism after the Revolution cut ties with the Church of England. The Baltimore Christmas Conference of 1784 constituted the Methodist Episcopal Church, ordaining Asbury as the first American bishop. Asbury traveled 300,000 miles, organized the circuit rider system (preachers assigned to vast frontier territories), and grew the church from 15,000 to 214,000 members during his episcopate.

The 1844 split over Bishop James Andrew's slave ownership was the most consequential ecclesiastical division in American religious history — creating the Methodist Episcopal Church (North) and Methodist Episcopal Church, South (MEC-South). The split demonstrated that no major institution — not churches, not political parties, not families — could remain unified over the slavery question. The northern MEC's General Conference provided institutional support for abolition and Black education; Freedmen's Aid Society schools founded by northern Methodists became historically Black colleges including Clark Atlanta, Rust, and Wiley College.
